The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere $S^3$. A **Seifert surface** for $K$ is a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface $F\subset S^3$ with boundary set equal to $K$. Orient each boundary component so that an outward-pointing conormal in $F$, followed by a positive boundary tangent, is a positive basis of $TF$; the oriented boundary of $F$ must agree with the given orientation of $K$. For such a surface, its genus $g(F)$ is the unique nonnegative integer satisfying $\chi(F)=2-2g(F)-b$, where $b$ is the number of boundary components; here $b=1$, so $\chi(F)=1-2g(F)$. The compact-surface normal-form result supplies this integer under the stated choice axiom.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K:S^1\hookrightarrow S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere, and let $F\subset S^3$ be a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface with boundary $K$, oriented so that its boundary orientation is the given orientation of $K$. Let $g$ be the nonnegative integer determined by $\chi(F)=1-2g$. Choose an ordered integral basis $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ of the first singular homology group $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$, represented by integral one-cycles on $F$. Orient the normal line of $F$ by requiring $(n,u,v)$ to be positively oriented in $S^3$ whenever $(u,v)$ is a positive tangent basis of $F$. The positive push-off $a_i^+$ is the cycle carried to a sufficiently small positive normal level in a bicollar of $F$.

For disjoint oriented closed curves $J,L\subset S^3$, orient a meridian $\mu_L$ of $L$ so that a positive tangent to $L$ followed by a positive basis of its normal disk gives the ambient orientation. The linking number $\operatorname{lk}(J,L)$ is the integer determined by $[J]=\operatorname{lk}(J,L)[\mu_L]$ in $H_1(S^3\setminus L;\mathbb Z)$, using the Alexander-duality identification that sends $[\mu_L]$ to $1$. Extend linking additively over integral one-cycles. The Seifert pairing is $\theta_F(x,y)=\operatorname{lk}(x^+,y)$, and its matrix in the chosen basis is $V=(V_{ij})_{i,j=1}^{2g}$, where $V_{ij}=\theta_F(a_i,a_j)=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. The surface and basis are part of the data; this definition asserts no knot-only matrix invariant.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $L=K_1\cup\cdots\cup K_r\subset S^3$ be an
oriented link with $r\ge1$ components and complement $X_L$,
([[def-oriented-link-in-s-three-and-ambient-isotopy]]), and let
$$\varphi:H_1(X_L;\mathbb Z)\longrightarrow\mathbb Z$$
be the **total linking homomorphism**, defined as the composite
$$H_1(X_L;\mathbb Z)\xrightarrow[\ \sim\ ]{\mathrm{Alex}}\widetilde H^1(L;\mathbb Z)\cong\bigoplus_{i=1}^rH^1(K_i;\mathbb Z)\xrightarrow{\text{sum}}\mathbb Z,$$
where the first arrow is Alexander duality
([[thm-alexander-duality-for-compact-locally-contractible-subsets-of-a-sphere]]),
each $H^1(K_i;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$ is the orientation-induced
identification, and the last map sums the $r$ coordinates. By
[[prop-the-first-hurewicz-map-in-degree-one-is-abelianization]] the map $\varphi$
may again be written $\pi_1(X_L)\to H_1(X_L)\xrightarrow{\varphi}\mathbb Z$; we
denote both composites by $\varphi$ and set $K:=\ker\varphi$.

The **one-variable Alexander module** of $L$ is
$$A_L:=H_1(\widetilde{X_L};\mathbb Z),$$
the first singular homology of the connected infinite cyclic cover
$p:\widetilde{X_L}\to X_L$ classified by $K$
([[thm-classification-of-connected-covering-spaces]],
[[lem-subgroup-quotient-of-universal-cover]],
[[def-covering-map-and-evenly-covered-neighbourhoods]]), equipped with its
structure of module over $\Lambda=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$
([[def-the-laurent-polynomial-ring]]) in which $t$ acts by the deck
transformation corresponding to the positive generator of
$\operatorname{Deck}(\widetilde{X_L}/X_L)\cong\mathbb Z$.

**Caveats.** The cover is the one classified by $K=\ker\varphi$; since $K$ is
normal the cover is regular and its deck group is
$\pi_1(X_L)/K\cong\mathbb Z$
([[def-regular-covering]], [[thm-regular-covering-characterizations]], [[cor-deck-group-of-a-regular-covering]],
[[def-deck-transformation-and-deck-group]]). The module $A_L$ is ordinary
integral homology of the cover, with the deck action as its module structure;
no twisting by a representation of the link group is used. The total linking
homomorphism satisfies $\varphi(\mu_i)=1$ for a meridian $\mu_i$ of any one
component, so $r\ge1$ is needed for $\varphi$ to be interesting and $A_L$
depends on the orientations of all components through this map.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, so that the Alexander module $A_L$ of an oriented
nonempty link $L$ is defined and finitely presented over
$\Lambda=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$
([[def-one-variable-alexander-module-of-an-oriented-link]],
[[lem-the-alexander-module-of-a-link-complement-is-finitely-presented]]). Let
$r$ be the number of components of $L$. Define the **one-variable Alexander
polynomial** $\Delta_L(t)\in\Lambda$ to be a greatest common divisor of the zeroth
elementary ideal $E_0(A_L)$
([[def-elementary-ideals-of-a-finitely-presented-module]]), i.e. a generator of
the smallest principal ideal of $\Lambda$ containing $E_0(A_L)$
([[lem-the-laurent-polynomial-ring-is-noetherian-and-a-unique-factorisation-domain]],
[[def-unique-factorisation-domain]]); it is well defined up to multiplication
by a unit $\pm t^k$ of $\Lambda$
([[lem-units-and-powers-of-the-laurent-polynomial-ring]]). The **Alexander
invariant** is the normalisation
$$D_L(t):=\begin{cases}\Delta_L(t),&r>1,\\[2pt] \dfrac{\Delta_L(t)}{1-t},&r=1,\end{cases}$$
understood for a knot as an element of the fraction field of $\Lambda$ when
$(1-t)\nmid\Delta_L(t)$; for the integer-valued link formulas of this page the
distinction matters and is stated with each use.

**Caveats.** The ideal $E_0(A_L)$ is a well-defined invariant of $L$ because
$A_L$ is finitely presented and elementary ideals are independent of the
presentation
([[lem-elementary-ideals-are-independent-of-the-presentation]]); a greatest
common divisor in a unique factorisation domain is well defined up to units, and
the units of $\Lambda$ are $\pm t^k$. For every link the absolute one-variable Alexander module admits a square
presentation, so $E_0(A_L)$ is principal, generated by its determinant (the
standard link fact recorded in [F3]). For a knot ($r=1$), every gcd
representative satisfies $\Delta_L(1)=\pm1$. These standard presentation and
normalisation facts are recorded here; the gcd definition itself uses only
finite presentability and unique factorisation.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring ([[def-commutative-ring]]) and let $M$ be a
finitely presented $R$-module ([[def-finitely-presented-module-and-algebra]]),
so that there are $m,n\in\mathbb N$ and a presentation

$$R^m\xrightarrow{\ A\ }R^n\xrightarrow{\ \beta\ }M\longrightarrow0 .$$

Fix the standard bases $e_1,\dots,e_m$ of $R^m$ and $f_1,\dots,f_n$ of $R^n$
([[def-finitely-presented-module-and-algebra]]) and let $A=(a_{ij})$ be the
$n\times m$ matrix of the $R$-linear map $\alpha$ with respect to them: the
$j$-th column of $A$ is the coordinate vector of $\alpha(e_j)$, so
$\alpha(e_j)=\sum_{i=1}^n a_{ij}f_i$. Such a matrix is called a **presentation
matrix** of $M$ (for the chosen presentation). A **minor** of $A$ of size
$r\times r$ is the determinant $\det(a_{i_sj_t})_{s,t=1}^r$
([[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]]) of the square submatrix obtained by
choosing rows $i_1<\dots<i_r$ and columns $j_1<\dots<j_r$; determinants of
$1\times1$ and $0\times0$ submatrices are allowed, with the empty determinant
equal to $1$.

For $k\ge0$ the **$k$-th elementary ideal** $E_k(M)$ of the presented module $M$
is the ideal of $R$ generated by the determinants of **all**
$(n-k)\times(n-k)$ minors of $A$ ([[def-generated-and-principal-ideals]],
[[def-left-right-and-two-sided-ideal]]): if $n-k>n$ or $n-k>m$ there is no such
minor, and the ideal generated by the empty set is $0$. In particular no minor
is nonzero-by-convention: the conventions are
$$E_k(M)=R\quad\text{for }k\ge n,\qquad E_k(M)=0\quad\text{for }k<n-m .$$
For $0\le k\le\min(n,m)$ the ideal $E_k(M)$ is the ideal generated by the
$(n-k)\times(n-k)$ minors; e.g. $E_1(M)$ is generated by the
$(n-1)\times(n-1)$ minors of $A$, and $E_n(M)=R$ because the $0\times0$ minor
is $1$. This is the $k$-th **Fitting ideal** $\operatorname{Fit}_k(M)$ of the
Stacks Project (Tag 07Z6, Lemma 15.8.2 and Definition 15.8.3), which is
indexed by the size $n-k$ of the complementary minors; the two conventions
$0=E_{-1}\subset E_0\subset\cdots$ agree on the range $0\le k\le\min(n,m)$.

**Caveats.** (i) The notation $E_k(M)$ suppresses the chosen presentation; the
ideal defined here is a priori attached to the presentation and it is the
content of [[lem-elementary-ideals-are-independent-of-the-presentation]] that
it is in fact an invariant of $M$. (ii) The conventions in the degenerate
ranges are conventions, not theorems; they are the ones compatible with the
Stacks numbering and with independence of the presentation.

Let $\mathbb Z[t]$ be the polynomial ring over the integers
([[def-polynomial-ring-over-a-commutative-ring]],
[[thm-polynomial-ring-is-a-commutative-ring]]) and let
$$S=\{t^k:k\ge0\}.$$
The set $S$ is multiplicative, and the **Laurent polynomial ring** is the
principal localisation
$$\Lambda_1:=\mathbb Z[t]_S=S^{-1}\mathbb Z[t]$$
([[def-principal-localisation]], [[def-multiplicative-subset-and-localisation]]).
It is a commutative ring with unit $1=t^0$ ([[def-commutative-ring]]). Write
again $t$ for the image of the indeterminate under the localisation map; then
$t$ is a unit with inverse $t^{-1}$
([[prop-units-in-a-localisation]]). Every element of $\Lambda_1$ has a
representative
$$\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}a_kt^k,\qquad a_k\in\mathbb Z,$$
with only finitely many nonzero coefficients, obtained by writing a fraction
$p/t^N$ as a finite $\mathbb Z$-linear combination of the powers
$t^{k-N}$; the finite coefficient sequence is unique: after multiplying two such sums
by a common sufficiently large power of $t$, equality becomes equality of
ordinary polynomials. The localisation map $\mathbb Z[t]\to\Lambda_1$ is
injective because $\mathbb Z[t]$ is a domain; hence their coefficients agree
([[cor-polynomial-ring-over-a-domain-is-a-domain]]). Equivalently, two such
sums are equal exactly when their coefficient sequences agree
([[prop-localisation-zero-equality-and-kernel-criteria]]).

**Universal property.** Let $A$ be a ring with unit and let
$\varphi\colon\mathbb Z[t]\to A$ be a unital ring homomorphism with
$\varphi(t)$ a unit of $A$. Then there is a unique unital ring homomorphism
$\widetilde\varphi\colon\Lambda_1\to A$ with
$\widetilde\varphi(t)=\varphi(t)$. Equivalently, for every unital ring $A$ and
every unit $u\in A$ there is a unique unital ring homomorphism
$\Lambda_1\to A$ with $t\mapsto u$ ([[thm-universal-property-of-localisation]],
[[def-ring-homomorphism]]).

The cited localisation theorem treats commutative target rings. For the
possibly noncommutative target used here, define
$\sum_k a_kt^k\mapsto\sum_k(a_k1_A)u^k$. Unique Laurent coefficients make
this well defined. Integer multiples of $1_A$ are central, and
$u^ku^l=u^{k+l}$ for all integers $k,l$, so finite distributivity proves
additivity, multiplicativity and preservation of $1$. Every unital
homomorphism must send $a_k$ to $a_k1_A$ and $t^k$ to $u^k$, proving
uniqueness. Taking $u=\varphi(t)$ gives the asserted extension of $\varphi$.

**Augmentation.** There is a unique unital ring homomorphism
$$\varepsilon\colon\Lambda_1\longrightarrow\mathbb Z,\qquad \varepsilon\Bigl(\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}a_kt^k\Bigr)=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}a_k,$$
the **sum-of-coefficients map** ([[thm-universal-property-of-localisation]]); it
is well defined because the coefficients are summable and their total sum is
unchanged along the relation of
[[prop-localisation-zero-equality-and-kernel-criteria]]. Its kernel is the
principal ideal $(t-1)$: indeed $\varepsilon(t-1)=0$, and if
$\varepsilon(x)=0$ then, writing $x=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}a_kt^k$ with finite
support and using that $\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}a_k=0$, one has
$$x=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}a_k(t^k-1)=(t-1)\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}a_k\,(1+t+\cdots+t^{k-1}),$$
where $1+t+\cdots+t^{k-1}$ denotes the empty sum $0$ for $k=0$ and, for
$k=-j<0$, the negative sum
$-(t^{-1}+t^{-2}+\cdots+t^{-j})$, so that
$t^{-j}-1=-(t-1)(t^{-1}+\cdots+t^{-j})$; hence $x\in(t-1)$, and the reverse
inclusion is $\varepsilon(t-1)=0$.

**Caveats.** This item realises $\Lambda_1$ by localisation and does **not**
identify it with an integral group ring: the additive group underlying
$\Lambda_1$ is $\bigoplus_{k\in\mathbb Z}\mathbb Z\,t^k$ and its multiplication
is the polynomial one ([[cor-polynomial-ring-over-a-domain-is-a-domain]] is not
needed for the ring laws but records that $\mathbb Z[t]$ is a domain). The
deck-module structures on homology introduced later on this page are defined
separately, by the universal property above.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $M$ be a finitely presented $R$-module.
Then for every $k\ge0$ the elementary ideal $E_k(M)$ of
[[def-elementary-ideals-of-a-finitely-presented-module]] is independent of the
chosen finite presentation of $M$; in particular it is an invariant of the
isomorphism class of $M$, and isomorphic modules have the same elementary
ideals.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in the oriented standard three-sphere, let $F$ be a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface with boundary orientation equal to that of $K$, let $g$ satisfy $\chi(F)=1-2g$, and choose an ordered integral basis $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$. Use the positive normal convention $(n,u,v)>0$ and define $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. Let $A_K=H_1(\widetilde X_K;\mathbb Z)$ be the one-variable Alexander module of the knot complement $X_K=S^3\setminus K$, where the cover is classified by the total-linking homomorphism and $t$ acts by the deck transformation corresponding to the positive meridian. Then there is an isomorphism of $\Lambda=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$-modules
$$A_K\cong\operatorname{coker}\bigl(V-tV^T:\Lambda^{2g}\to\Lambda^{2g}\bigr).$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented embedded circle in the oriented standard three-sphere, let $F$ be a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface with boundary $K$, and let $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ be any ordered integral basis of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$ with Seifert matrix $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. Let $J_F$ be the matrix of the algebraic intersection form on $F$, with a transverse intersection of oriented curves $u,v$ counted positively exactly when their ordered tangent vectors form a positive basis of $TF$. Then $V-V^T=J_F$. The matrix $J_F$ is skew-symmetric and unimodular; when $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ is a standard handle basis, it is a direct sum of blocks $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $(K,F)$ and $(K',F')$ be oriented knot and spanning-surface pairs in the oriented standard three-sphere, and let $h_t:S^3\to S^3$ be a smooth ambient isotopy with $h_0$ the identity, $h_1(K)=K'$, and $h_1(F)=F'$, preserving the given orientations. If $V$ and $V'$ are their Seifert matrices in any integral bases, then the basis transported by $h_1$ has matrix $V$, and any other target basis with transition matrix $P$ has matrix $V'=P^TVP$. Hence $V$ and $V'$ are S-equivalent, meaning they are related by a finite sequence of integral unimodular congruences and the two elementary rank-two enlargement moves or their reverses.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $L$ and $L'$ be nonempty oriented links in $S^3$ such
that some ambient isotopy of $S^3$ carries $L$ onto $L'$ and preserves the
orientations of the components
([[def-oriented-link-in-s-three-and-ambient-isotopy]]). Then the Alexander
modules $A_L$ and $A_{L'}$ of
[[def-one-variable-alexander-module-of-an-oriented-link]] are isomorphic as
$\Lambda$-modules over $\Lambda=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$, their zeroth elementary
ideals agree, $E_0(A_L)=E_0(A_{L'})$, and consequently the one-variable
Alexander polynomials of
[[def-alexander-polynomial-from-the-first-elementary-ideal]] satisfy
$$\Delta_{L'}(t)=\pm t^{k}\,\Delta_L(t)\quad\text{for some }k\in\mathbb Z;$$
so the oriented link type of $L$ determines $\Delta_L$ up to multiplication by
a unit $\pm t^k$ of $\Lambda$ (and, for knots, the Alexander invariant
$D_L=\Delta_L/(1-t)$ up to the same unit).

derivations.claim: Put $n=2g$ and $M(t)=V-tV^T$. By [F1] this is the positive-push matrix in the Statement, and by [F4] $A_K$ is isomorphic to the cokernel of the square presentation matrix $M(t)$. The definition of $E_0$ uses the $n\times n$ minors; the only such minor of an $n\times n$ matrix is its determinant. Thus the presentation gives $E_0(\operatorname{coker}M)=(\det M)$, including $n=0$, where the sole empty minor is $1$. Presentation and isomorphism independence [F3] yields $E_0(A_K)=(\det M)$.

Evaluating at $t=1$ gives $\det M(1)=\det(V-V^T)=\det J_F=\pm1$ by [F5]. Since $E_0(A_K)=(\det M)$ and $\Delta_K$ is a generator of that principal ideal, $\Delta_K=u\det M$ for a unit $u=\pm t^k$ by [F2]; every such unit evaluates to $\pm1$ at $t=1$. Hence $\Delta_K(1)=\pm1$.

If the basis is changed by $P\in\mathrm{GL}_{n}(\mathbb Z)$, then $M'(t)=P^TM(t)P$ and $\det M'=(\det P)^2\det M=\det M$. Under an ambient isotopy, [F6] gives this same transported-matrix relation and [F7] preserves the Alexander ideal up to its unit generator. Thus the asserted ideal-generator relation is compatible with the stated choices.

Then the square matrix $M(t)=V-tV^T$ generates that ideal:

$$E_0(A_K)=(\det M(t)).$$

For $g=0$, the matrix is empty and its determinant is $1$. In every genus, $\det(V-V^T)=\pm1$, so every generator $\Delta_K$ satisfies $\Delta_K(1)=\pm1$. Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $L=K_1\cup\cdots\cup K_r\subset S^3$ be an
oriented link with $r\ge1$ components and complement $X_L$,
([[def-oriented-link-in-s-three-and-ambient-isotopy]]), and let
$$\varphi:H_1(X_L;\mathbb Z)\longrightarrow\mathbb Z$$
be the **total linking homomorphism**, defined as the composite
$$H_1(X_L;\mathbb Z)\xrightarrow[\ \sim\ ]{\mathrm{Alex}}\widetilde H^1(L;\mathbb Z)\cong\bigoplus_{i=1}^rH^1(K_i;\mathbb Z)\xrightarrow{\text{sum}}\mathbb Z,$$
where the first arrow is Alexander duality
([[thm-alexander-duality-for-compact-locally-contractible-subsets-of-a-sphere]]),
each $H^1(K_i;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$ is the orientation-induced
identification, and the last map sums the $r$ coordinates. By
[[prop-the-first-hurewicz-map-in-degree-one-is-abelianization]] the map $\varphi$
may again be written $\pi_1(X_L)\to H_1(X_L)\xrightarrow{\varphi}\mathbb Z$; we
denote both composites by $\varphi$ and set $K:=\ker\varphi$.

The **one-variable Alexander module** of $L$ is
$$A_L:=H_1(\widetilde{X_L};\mathbb Z),$$
the first singular homology of the connected infinite cyclic cover
$p:\widetilde{X_L}\to X_L$ classified by $K$
([[thm-classification-of-connected-covering-spaces]],
[[lem-subgroup-quotient-of-universal-cover]],
[[def-covering-map-and-evenly-covered-neighbourhoods]]), equipped with its
structure of module over $\Lambda=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$
([[def-the-laurent-polynomial-ring]]) in which $t$ acts by the deck
transformation corresponding to the positive generator of
$\operatorname{Deck}(\widetilde{X_L}/X_L)\cong\mathbb Z$.

normal the cover is regular and its deck group is
$\pi_1(X_L)/K\cong\mathbb Z$
([[def-regular-covering]], [[thm-regular-covering-characterizations]], [[cor-deck-group-of-a-regular-covering]],

integral homology of the cover, with the deck action as its module structure;

homomorphism satisfies $\varphi(\mu_i)=1$ for a meridian $\mu_i$ of any one

depends on the orientations of all components through this map.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, so that the Alexander module $A_L$ of an oriented
nonempty link $L$ is defined and finitely presented over
$\Lambda=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$
([[def-one-variable-alexander-module-of-an-oriented-link]],
[[lem-the-alexander-module-of-a-link-complement-is-finitely-presented]]). Let

([[def-elementary-ideals-of-a-finitely-presented-module]]), i.e. a generator of

([[lem-the-laurent-polynomial-ring-is-noetherian-and-a-unique-factorisation-domain]],

([[lem-units-and-powers-of-the-laurent-polynomial-ring]]). The **Alexander

$$D_L(t):=\begin{cases}\Delta_L(t),&r>1,\\[2pt] \dfrac{\Delta_L(t)}{1-t},&r=1,\end{cases}$$

$$S=\{t^k:k\ge0\}.$$

principal localisation
$$\Lambda_1:=\mathbb Z[t]_S=S^{-1}\mathbb Z[t]$$
([[def-principal-localisation]], [[def-multiplicative-subset-and-localisation]]).

again $t$ for the image of the indeterminate under the localisation map; then
$t$ is a unit with inverse $t^{-1}$
([[prop-units-in-a-localisation]]). Every element of $\Lambda_1$ has a
representative
$$\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}a_kt^k,\qquad a_k\in\mathbb Z,$$
with only finitely many nonzero coefficients, obtained by writing a fraction
$p/t^N$ as a finite $\mathbb Z$-linear combination of the powers
$t^{k-N}$; the finite coefficient sequence is unique: after multiplying two such sums
by a common sufficiently large power of $t$, equality becomes equality of
ordinary polynomials. The localisation map $\mathbb Z[t]\to\Lambda_1$ is
injective because $\mathbb Z[t]$ is a domain; hence their coefficients agree
([[cor-polynomial-ring-over-a-domain-is-a-domain]]). Equivalently, two such
sums are equal exactly when their coefficient sequences agree
([[prop-localisation-zero-equality-and-kernel-criteria]]).

**Universal property.** Let $A$ be a ring with unit and let
$\varphi\colon\mathbb Z[t]\to A$ be a unital ring homomorphism with
$\varphi(t)$ a unit of $A$. Then there is a unique unital ring homomorphism
$\widetilde\varphi\colon\Lambda_1\to A$ with
$\widetilde\varphi(t)=\varphi(t)$. Equivalently, for every unital ring $A$ and
every unit $u\in A$ there is a unique unital ring homomorphism
$\Lambda_1\to A$ with $t\mapsto u$ ([[thm-universal-property-of-localisation]],
[[def-ring-homomorphism]]).

The cited localisation theorem treats commutative target rings. For the
possibly noncommutative target used here, define
$\sum_k a_kt^k\mapsto\sum_k(a_k1_A)u^k$. Unique Laurent coefficients make
this well defined. Integer multiples of $1_A$ are central, and
$u^ku^l=u^{k+l}$ for all integers $k,l$, so finite distributivity proves
additivity, multiplicativity and preservation of $1$. Every unital
homomorphism must send $a_k$ to $a_k1_A$ and $t^k$ to $u^k$, proving
uniqueness. Taking $u=\varphi(t)$ gives the asserted extension of $\varphi$.

**Augmentation.** There is a unique unital ring homomorphism
$$\varepsilon\colon\Lambda_1\longrightarrow\mathbb Z,\qquad \varepsilon\Bigl(\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}a_kt^k\Bigr)=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}a_k,$$
the **sum-of-coefficients map** ([[thm-universal-property-of-localisation]]); it
is well defined because the coefficients are summable and their total sum is
unchanged along the relation of
[[prop-localisation-zero-equality-and-kernel-criteria]]. Its kernel is the
principal ideal $(t-1)$: indeed $\varepsilon(t-1)=0$, and if
$\varepsilon(x)=0$ then, writing $x=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}a_kt^k$ with finite
support and using that $\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}a_k=0$, one has
$$x=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}a_k(t^k-1)=(t-1)\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}a_k\,(1+t+\cdots+t^{k-1}),$$
where $1+t+\cdots+t^{k-1}$ denotes the empty sum $0$ for $k=0$ and, for
$k=-j<0$, the negative sum
$-(t^{-1}+t^{-2}+\cdots+t^{-j})$, so that
$t^{-j}-1=-(t-1)(t^{-1}+\cdots+t^{-j})$; hence $x\in(t-1)$, and the reverse
inclusion is $\varepsilon(t-1)=0$.

**Caveats.** This item realises $\Lambda_1$ by localisation and does **not**
identify it with an integral group ring: the additive group underlying
$\Lambda_1$ is $\bigoplus_{k\in\mathbb Z}\mathbb Z\,t^k$ and its multiplication
is the polynomial one ([[cor-polynomial-ring-over-a-domain-is-a-domain]] is not
needed for the ring laws but records that $\mathbb Z[t]$ is a domain). The
deck-module structures on homology introduced later on this page are defined
separately, by the universal property above.

([[def-oriented-link-in-s-three-and-ambient-isotopy]]). Then the Alexander

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in the oriented standard three-sphere, let $F$ be a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface with boundary orientation equal to that of $K$, let $g$ satisfy $\chi(F)=1-2g$, and choose an ordered integral basis $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$. Use the positive normal convention $(n,u,v)>0$ and define $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. Let $A_K=H_1(\widetilde X_K;\mathbb Z)$ be the one-variable Alexander module of the knot complement $X_K=S^3\setminus K$, where the cover is classified by the total-linking homomorphism and $t$ acts by the deck transformation corresponding to the positive meridian. Then there is an isomorphism of $\Lambda=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$-modules
$$A_K\cong\operatorname{coker}\bigl(V-tV^T:\Lambda^{2g}\to\Lambda^{2g}\bigr).$$

Assume the full Axiom of Choice. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot, and let $F\subset S^3$ be a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface whose oriented boundary is $K$, with $\chi(F)=1-2g$. Choose an ordered integral basis $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$ and use the positive normal convention $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. Let $A_K$ be the first homology of the infinite cyclic cover of $S^3\setminus K$ classified by total linking, with $t$ acting by the positive-meridian deck transformation. Let $\Delta_K(t)$ be the generator of the zeroth elementary ideal $E_0(A_K)$ in $\Lambda=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$, and write $p\doteq q$ when $p$ and $q$ differ by a unit $\pm t^k$ of $\Lambda$. Then for every such $F$ and basis,

$$\det(V-tV^T)\doteq\Delta_K(t).$$

The determinant is $1$ for the empty $0\times0$ matrix when $g=0$. This formula concerns the polynomial $\Delta_K$; the existing knot-normalized fraction $D_K=\Delta_K/(1-t)$ is a separate invariant.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For disjoint oriented closed curves $J,L\subset S^3$, orient a meridian $\mu_L$ of $L$ so that a positive tangent to $L$ followed by a positive basis of its normal disk gives the ambient orientation. The linking number $\operatorname{lk}(J,L)$ is the integer determined by $[J]=\operatorname{lk}(J,L)[\mu_L]$ in $H_1(S^3\setminus L;\mathbb Z)$, using the Alexander-duality identification that sends $[\mu_L]$ to $1$. The Seifert pairing is $\theta_F(x,y)=\operatorname{lk}(x^+,y)$, and its matrix in the chosen basis is $V=(V_{ij})_{i,j=1}^{2g}$, where $V_{ij}=\theta_F(a_i,a_j)=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For an oriented smooth knot $K\subset S^3$, define

$$\mathcal G(K):=\{n\in\mathbb N_0: \text{there is a Seifert surface }F\text{ for }K\text{ with }g(F)=n\}.$$

Every element of $\mathcal G(K)$ is the genus of a connected compact oriented surface. The existence theorem makes $\mathcal G(K)$ nonempty, and the well-ordering of $\mathbb N_0$ gives its least element. The **smooth knot genus** is $g(K):=\min\mathcal G(K)$. This genus is the minimum over embedded spanning surfaces; it is not the number of Seifert circles or the genus of every surface produced from a diagram.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere $S^3$. A **Seifert surface** for $K$ is a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface $F\subset S^3$ with boundary set equal to $K$. Orient each boundary component so that an outward-pointing conormal in $F$, followed by a positive boundary tangent, is a positive basis of $TF$; the oriented boundary of $F$ must agree with the given orientation of $K$. For such a surface, its genus $g(F)$ is the unique nonnegative integer satisfying $\chi(F)=2-2g(F)-b$, where $b$ is the number of boundary components; here $b=1$, so $\chi(F)=1-2g(F)$. The compact-surface normal-form result supplies this integer under the stated choice axiom.

([[def-polynomial-ring-over-a-commutative-ring]],
[[thm-polynomial-ring-is-a-commutative-ring]]) and let
$$S=\{t^k:k\ge0\}.$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Fix a coordinate orientation-reversing reflection $r:S^3\to S^3$ for the mirror convention. Let $K$ and $J$ be smooth oriented knots in the standard oriented three-sphere. A connected-sum datum consists of one smoothly embedded closed three-ball around a short subarc of $K$ and one around a short subarc of $J$, each meeting its knot in a single trivial properly embedded arc, together with the fixed standard orientation-reversing boundary identification of the two standard oriented ball boundaries that joins the oriented arcs into one circle. Choose this standard map once in the standard two-ball model so that it commutes with $r$ and an orientation-preserving half-turn interchanging the two balls preserves the joining convention. Here a trivial arc is an embedded interval in a ball that is carried by an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism of ball-arc pairs to a straight diameter. Remove the interiors of the two balls and glue the remaining boundary spheres using this fixed identification; the resulting oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere is a connected sum of $K$ and $J$, denoted $K\#J$ for the specified datum.

The **standard unknot** is the counterclockwise circle $U=\{(x_1,x_2,0)\in\mathbb R^3:x_1^2+x_2^2=1\}\subset S^3=\mathbb R^3\cup\{\infty\}$. Under inverse stereographic projection $x\mapsto(2x/(1+\lVert x\rVert^2),(\lVert x\rVert^2-1)/(1+\lVert x\rVert^2))$, this is the unit circle in the first coordinate two-plane of the unit sphere in $\mathbb R^4$. A knot is **nontrivial** if it is not ambient isotopic through orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms of $S^3$ to the standard unknot. A nontrivial knot is **prime** if it has no connected-sum presentation whose two summand knots are both nontrivial.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For two smooth oriented knots, changing either representative by oriented ambient isotopy, changing the sufficiently small coordinate ball and trivial subarc used for either knot, or changing the positive local frame used to identify that ball with the standard oriented ball does not change the oriented ambient-isotopy class of the connected-sum knot, when the boundary gluing map is the fixed standard orientation-reversing map from the definition.

For such a surface, its genus $g(F)$ is the unique nonnegative integer satisfying $\chi(F)=2-2g(F)-b$, where $b$ is the number of boundary components; here $b=1$, so $\chi(F)=1-2g(F)$. The compact-surface normal-form result supplies this integer under the stated choice axiom.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice-principle-for-foliation-pair]]). Let $S$ be an oriented Hausdorff $C^2$ surface without boundary, possibly disconnected. Then:

1. Every compact subset $K\subset S$ lies in the interior of a compact finitely cellulated $C^2$ subsurface $N$. If $K$ is contained in one connected component of $S$, $N$ can be chosen connected. 2. Every connected closed compact subsurface has an oriented genus normal form: the sphere for $g=0$, or the polygon word $\prod_{i=1}^g a_i b_i a_i^{-1}b_i^{-1}$ for $g\ge1$, with $\chi=2-2g$. 4. Every regular embedded $C^2$ nullhomotopic circle $c$ bounds an embedded compact disk region in $S$. Here a disk region is a compact subsurface homeomorphic to the closed disk, with boundary exactly $c$; its inherited surface structure and boundary are $C^2$. The normal forms in clause 2 are homeomorphism normal forms. No general differentiable smoothing theorem or arbitrary-surface triangulation-existence theorem is a premise of this item.

is surjective and has kernel $[\pi_1(X,x_0),\pi_1(X,x_0)]$. Hence it induces a natural isomorphism
$$\pi_1(X,x_0)^{\mathrm{ab}}\cong H_1(X;\mathbb Z).$$

Choose an ordered integral basis $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ of the first singular homology group $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$, represented by integral one-cycles on $F$. Orient the normal line of $F$ by requiring $(n,u,v)$ to be positively oriented in $S^3$ whenever $(u,v)$ is a positive tangent basis of $F$. ([[def-oriented-link-in-s-three-and-ambient-isotopy]]), and let
$$\varphi:H_1(X_L;\mathbb Z)\longrightarrow\mathbb Z$$

$$A_L:=H_1(\widetilde{X_L};\mathbb Z),$$

[[lem-subgroup-quotient-of-universal-cover]],
[[def-covering-map-and-evenly-covered-neighbourhoods]]), equipped with its

[[def-deck-transformation-and-deck-group]]). The module $A_L$ is ordinary

A connected compact subsurface with $b>0$ boundary circles has a free fundamental group; capping its boundaries defines genus $g$ and gives $\chi=2-2g-b$ and free rank $2g+b-1$.

proof_evidence.quote: 1.2 (A boundary surface has a finite graph spine.) Let $N$ be connected and $\partial N\ne\varnothing$, with the triangulation from F1. Its triangle dual graph, with an additional exterior vertex joined to triangles along their boundary edges, is connected: the cyclic or interval vertex links join all triangles incident to a vertex, and connectedness then joins all triangles. Choose a finite spanning tree rooted at the exterior vertex. Remove triangles in order from the root outward, always removing a triangle together with the edge connecting it to its already removed parent. That edge is free at its removal: its only other incident triangle has already been removed, or it was a boundary edge. A triangle with a free side strongly deformation retracts onto its other two sides; in coordinates on a planar reference triangle this is the elementary linear edge-collapse retraction. Performing these finitely many collapses leaves a connected finite embedded graph $B$, and $N$ deformation retracts onto $B$. More is true geometrically: $N$ is homeomorphic to a thickening of $B$. To check it, take small vertex disks and edge rectangles in the triangle charts. Reversing one free-side collapse attaches the missing triangular bulge along the two retained side strips. The union of those two strips and the bulge is a disk with the same two attaching arcs; parametrize its boundary arcs in the same order and extend their circle homeomorphism radially across the reference disk. This replaces the bulged neighborhood by the unbulged one relative to its attaching arcs. Induction reverses every collapse and identifies a neighborhood of the final graph with all of $N$, carrying boundary to boundary. Thus the thickening is made of finitely many vertex disks and edge bands with the orientation-induced cyclic orders. This argument proves the needed thickening assertion, rather than inferring it from a deformation retraction alone. [F1, construct]

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K:S^1\hookrightarrow S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere, and let $F\subset S^3$ be a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface with boundary $K$, oriented so that its boundary orientation is the given orientation of $K$. Let $g$ be the nonnegative integer determined by $\chi(F)=1-2g$. Choose an ordered integral basis $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ of the first singular homology group $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$, represented by integral one-cycles on $F$. Orient the normal line of $F$ by requiring $(n,u,v)$ to be positively oriented in $S^3$ whenever $(u,v)$ is a positive tangent basis of $F$. The positive push-off $a_i^+$ is the cycle carried to a sufficiently small positive normal level in a bicollar of $F$.

For disjoint oriented closed curves $J,L\subset S^3$, orient a meridian $\mu_L$ of $L$ so that a positive tangent to $L$ followed by a positive basis of its normal disk gives the ambient orientation. The linking number $\operatorname{lk}(J,L)$ is the integer determined by $[J]=\operatorname{lk}(J,L)[\mu_L]$ in $H_1(S^3\setminus L;\mathbb Z)$, using the Alexander-duality identification that sends $[\mu_L]$ to $1$. Extend linking additively over integral one-cycles. The Seifert pairing is $\theta_F(x,y)=\operatorname{lk}(x^+,y)$, and its matrix in the chosen basis is $V=(V_{ij})_{i,j=1}^{2g}$, where $V_{ij}=\theta_F(a_i,a_j)=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. The surface and basis are part of the data; this definition asserts no knot-only matrix invariant.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented embedded circle in the oriented standard three-sphere, let $F$ be a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface with boundary $K$, and let $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ be any ordered integral basis of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$ with Seifert matrix $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. Let $J_F$ be the matrix of the algebraic intersection form on $F$, with a transverse intersection of oriented curves $u,v$ counted positively exactly when their ordered tangent vectors form a positive basis of $TF$. Then $V-V^T=J_F$. The matrix $J_F$ is skew-symmetric and unimodular; when $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ is a standard handle basis, it is a direct sum of blocks $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere $S^3$. A **Seifert surface** for $K$ is a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface $F\subset S^3$ with boundary set equal to $K$. Orient each boundary component so that an outward-pointing conormal in $F$, followed by a positive boundary tangent, is a positive basis of $TF$; the oriented boundary of $F$ must agree with the given orientation of $K$. For such a surface, its genus $g(F)$ is the unique nonnegative integer satisfying $\chi(F)=2-2g(F)-b$, where $b$ is the number of boundary components; here $b=1$, so $\chi(F)=1-2g(F)$. The compact-surface normal-form result supplies this integer under the stated choice axiom.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice-principle-for-foliation-pair]]). Let $S$ be an oriented Hausdorff $C^2$ surface without boundary, possibly disconnected. Then:

1. Every compact subset $K\subset S$ lies in the interior of a compact finitely cellulated $C^2$ subsurface $N$. If $K$ is contained in one connected component of $S$, $N$ can be chosen connected. A specified finite embedded regular $C^2$ graph contained in $\operatorname{Int}N$ can be included in its one-skeleton.
2. Every connected closed compact subsurface has an oriented genus normal form: the sphere for $g=0$, or the polygon word $\prod_{i=1}^g a_i b_i a_i^{-1}b_i^{-1}$ for $g\ge1$, with $\chi=2-2g$. A connected compact subsurface with $b>0$ boundary circles has a free fundamental group; capping its boundaries defines genus $g$ and gives $\chi=2-2g-b$ and free rank $2g+b-1$.
3. The fundamental group of every connected component of $S$ is torsion-free.
4. Every regular embedded $C^2$ nullhomotopic circle $c$ bounds an embedded compact disk region in $S$. Here a disk region is a compact subsurface homeomorphic to the closed disk, with boundary exactly $c$; its inherited surface structure and boundary are $C^2$. It is unique unless the **connected component containing $c$** is a sphere; in that component the two complementary disk regions are the two possibilities.

The normal forms in clause 2 are homeomorphism normal forms. No general differentiable smoothing theorem or arbitrary-surface triangulation-existence theorem is a premise of this item.

For every path-connected topological space $X$ and $x_0\in X$, the Hurewicz map
$$h:\pi_1(X,x_0)\longrightarrow H_1(X;\mathbb Z)$$
is surjective and has kernel $[\pi_1(X,x_0),\pi_1(X,x_0)]$. Hence it induces a natural isomorphism
$$\pi_1(X,x_0)^{\mathrm{ab}}\cong H_1(X;\mathbb Z).$$
The proof is choice-free and requires no CW, separation, local path-connectivity or local simple-connectivity assumption.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $L=K_1\cup\cdots\cup K_r\subset S^3$ be an
oriented link with $r\ge1$ components and complement $X_L$,
([[def-oriented-link-in-s-three-and-ambient-isotopy]]), and let
$$\varphi:H_1(X_L;\mathbb Z)\longrightarrow\mathbb Z$$
be the **total linking homomorphism**, defined as the composite
$$H_1(X_L;\mathbb Z)\xrightarrow[\ \sim\ ]{\mathrm{Alex}}\widetilde H^1(L;\mathbb Z)\cong\bigoplus_{i=1}^rH^1(K_i;\mathbb Z)\xrightarrow{\text{sum}}\mathbb Z,$$
where the first arrow is Alexander duality
([[thm-alexander-duality-for-compact-locally-contractible-subsets-of-a-sphere]]),
each $H^1(K_i;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$ is the orientation-induced
identification, and the last map sums the $r$ coordinates. By
[[prop-the-first-hurewicz-map-in-degree-one-is-abelianization]] the map $\varphi$
may again be written $\pi_1(X_L)\to H_1(X_L)\xrightarrow{\varphi}\mathbb Z$; we
denote both composites by $\varphi$ and set $K:=\ker\varphi$.

The **one-variable Alexander module** of $L$ is
$$A_L:=H_1(\widetilde{X_L};\mathbb Z),$$
the first singular homology of the connected infinite cyclic cover
$p:\widetilde{X_L}\to X_L$ classified by $K$
([[thm-classification-of-connected-covering-spaces]],
[[lem-subgroup-quotient-of-universal-cover]],
[[def-covering-map-and-evenly-covered-neighbourhoods]]), equipped with its
structure of module over $\Lambda=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$
([[def-the-laurent-polynomial-ring]]) in which $t$ acts by the deck
transformation corresponding to the positive generator of
$\operatorname{Deck}(\widetilde{X_L}/X_L)\cong\mathbb Z$.

**Caveats.** The cover is the one classified by $K=\ker\varphi$; since $K$ is
normal the cover is regular and its deck group is
$\pi_1(X_L)/K\cong\mathbb Z$
([[def-regular-covering]], [[thm-regular-covering-characterizations]], [[cor-deck-group-of-a-regular-covering]],
[[def-deck-transformation-and-deck-group]]). The module $A_L$ is ordinary
integral homology of the cover, with the deck action as its module structure;
no twisting by a representation of the link group is used. The total linking
homomorphism satisfies $\varphi(\mu_i)=1$ for a meridian $\mu_i$ of any one
component, so $r\ge1$ is needed for $\varphi$ to be interesting and $A_L$
depends on the orientations of all components through this map.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, so that the Alexander module $A_L$ of an oriented
nonempty link $L$ is defined and finitely presented over
$\Lambda=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$
([[def-one-variable-alexander-module-of-an-oriented-link]],
[[lem-the-alexander-module-of-a-link-complement-is-finitely-presented]]). Let
$r$ be the number of components of $L$. Define the **one-variable Alexander
polynomial** $\Delta_L(t)\in\Lambda$ to be a greatest common divisor of the zeroth
elementary ideal $E_0(A_L)$
([[def-elementary-ideals-of-a-finitely-presented-module]]), i.e. a generator of
the smallest principal ideal of $\Lambda$ containing $E_0(A_L)$
([[lem-the-laurent-polynomial-ring-is-noetherian-and-a-unique-factorisation-domain]],
[[def-unique-factorisation-domain]]); it is well defined up to multiplication
by a unit $\pm t^k$ of $\Lambda$
([[lem-units-and-powers-of-the-laurent-polynomial-ring]]). The **Alexander
invariant** is the normalisation
$$D_L(t):=\begin{cases}\Delta_L(t),&r>1,\\[2pt] \dfrac{\Delta_L(t)}{1-t},&r=1,\end{cases}$$
understood for a knot as an element of the fraction field of $\Lambda$ when
$(1-t)\nmid\Delta_L(t)$; for the integer-valued link formulas of this page the
distinction matters and is stated with each use.

**Caveats.** The ideal $E_0(A_L)$ is a well-defined invariant of $L$ because
$A_L$ is finitely presented and elementary ideals are independent of the
presentation
([[lem-elementary-ideals-are-independent-of-the-presentation]]); a greatest
common divisor in a unique factorisation domain is well defined up to units, and
the units of $\Lambda$ are $\pm t^k$. For every link the absolute one-variable Alexander module admits a square
presentation, so $E_0(A_L)$ is principal, generated by its determinant (the
standard link fact recorded in [F3]). For a knot ($r=1$), every gcd
representative satisfies $\Delta_L(1)=\pm1$. These standard presentation and
normalisation facts are recorded here; the gcd definition itself uses only
finite presentability and unique factorisation.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in the oriented standard three-sphere, let $F$ be a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface with boundary orientation equal to that of $K$, let $g$ satisfy $\chi(F)=1-2g$, and choose an ordered integral basis $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$. Use the positive normal convention $(n,u,v)>0$ and define $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. Let $A_K=H_1(\widetilde X_K;\mathbb Z)$ be the one-variable Alexander module of the knot complement $X_K=S^3\setminus K$, where the cover is classified by the total-linking homomorphism and $t$ acts by the deck transformation corresponding to the positive meridian. Then there is an isomorphism of $\Lambda=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$-modules
$$A_K\cong\operatorname{coker}\bigl(V-tV^T:\Lambda^{2g}\to\Lambda^{2g}\bigr).$$

Assume the full Axiom of Choice. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot, let $F\subset S^3$ be a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface with oriented boundary $K$, and let $\chi(F)=1-2g$ with $g\ge0$. Choose an ordered integral basis $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$, use the positive normal convention, and set $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. Let $\Lambda=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$, let $A_K$ be the first homology of the infinite cyclic cover classified by total linking with $t$ acting by the positive-meridian deck transformation, and let $\Delta_K$ be a generator of the zeroth elementary ideal $E_0(A_K)$. Then the square matrix $M(t)=V-tV^T$ generates that ideal:

$$E_0(A_K)=(\det M(t)).$$

For $g=0$, the matrix is empty and its determinant is $1$. In every genus, $\det(V-V^T)=\pm1$, so every generator $\Delta_K$ satisfies $\Delta_K(1)=\pm1$. The ideal and determinant assertions are compatible with integral basis changes and with orientation-preserving ambient isotopies of knot-surface pairs.

Assume the full Axiom of Choice. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot, and let $F\subset S^3$ be a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface whose oriented boundary is $K$, with $\chi(F)=1-2g$. Choose an ordered integral basis $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$ and use the positive normal convention $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. Let $A_K$ be the first homology of the infinite cyclic cover of $S^3\setminus K$ classified by total linking, with $t$ acting by the positive-meridian deck transformation. Let $\Delta_K(t)$ be the generator of the zeroth elementary ideal $E_0(A_K)$ in $\Lambda=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$, and write $p\doteq q$ when $p$ and $q$ differ by a unit $\pm t^k$ of $\Lambda$. Then for every such $F$ and basis,

$$\det(V-tV^T)\doteq\Delta_K(t).$$

The determinant is $1$ for the empty $0\times0$ matrix when $g=0$. This formula concerns the polynomial $\Delta_K$; the existing knot-normalized fraction $D_K=\Delta_K/(1-t)$ is a separate invariant.

Assume the full Axiom of Choice and let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot. For a nonzero Laurent polynomial $f(t)=\sum_j c_jt^j$, define $\deg f=\max\{j:c_j\ne0\}-\min\{j:c_j\ne0\}$; this is its exponent width and is unchanged by multiplication by a unit $\pm t^k$. Let $g(K)$ be the minimum genus of a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface in $S^3$ with oriented boundary $K$, and let $\Delta_K$ be any generator of the zeroth elementary ideal of its one-variable Alexander module. Then every such generator satisfies

$$\Delta_K(1)=\pm1,\qquad \Delta_K(t^{-1})\doteq\Delta_K(t),\qquad \deg\Delta_K\le 2g(K),$$

where $\doteq$ means equality up to a unit $\pm t^k$. Consequently, there is a unique associate $\Delta_K^\#(t)$ with $\Delta_K^\#(1)=1$ and $\Delta_K^\#(t^{-1})=\Delta_K^\#(t)$; its exponent support is centered in $[-g(K),g(K)]$. Under the existing convention the knot-normalized fraction $D_K(t)=\Delta_K(t)/(1-t)$ is distinct from the polynomial $\Delta_K$; because $\Delta_K(1)=\pm1$, it has a simple pole at $t=1$.

Assume the full Axiom of Choice. Let $K,J\subset S^3$ be smooth oriented knots, and let $K\#J$ be their oriented connected sum for a connected-sum datum using the fixed gluing convention. Then

$$\Delta_{K\#J}(t)\doteq \Delta_K(t)\Delta_J(t),$$

where each $\Delta$ is the generator of the zeroth elementary ideal of the one-variable Alexander module and $\doteq$ means equality up to multiplication by a unit $\pm t^k$ of $\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$. The statement is independent of the local connected-sum choices and of the Seifert surfaces and bases used to compute the polynomials.

Fix a coordinate orientation-reversing reflection $r:S^3\to S^3$ for the mirror convention. Let $K$ and $J$ be smooth oriented knots in the standard oriented three-sphere. A connected-sum datum consists of one smoothly embedded closed three-ball around a short subarc of $K$ and one around a short subarc of $J$, each meeting its knot in a single trivial properly embedded arc, together with the fixed standard orientation-reversing boundary identification of the two standard oriented ball boundaries that joins the oriented arcs into one circle. Choose this standard map once in the standard two-ball model so that it commutes with $r$ and an orientation-preserving half-turn interchanging the two balls preserves the joining convention. Here a trivial arc is an embedded interval in a ball that is carried by an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism of ball-arc pairs to a straight diameter. Remove the interiors of the two balls and glue the remaining boundary spheres using this fixed identification; the resulting oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere is a connected sum of $K$ and $J$, denoted $K\#J$ for the specified datum.

The **standard unknot** is the counterclockwise circle $U=\{(x_1,x_2,0)\in\mathbb R^3:x_1^2+x_2^2=1\}\subset S^3=\mathbb R^3\cup\{\infty\}$. Under inverse stereographic projection $x\mapsto(2x/(1+\lVert x\rVert^2),(\lVert x\rVert^2-1)/(1+\lVert x\rVert^2))$, this is the unit circle in the first coordinate two-plane of the unit sphere in $\mathbb R^4$. A knot is **nontrivial** if it is not ambient isotopic through orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms of $S^3$ to the standard unknot. A nontrivial knot is **prime** if it has no connected-sum presentation whose two summand knots are both nontrivial.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $(K,F)$ and $(K',F')$ be oriented knot and spanning-surface pairs in the oriented standard three-sphere, and let $h_t:S^3\to S^3$ be a smooth ambient isotopy with $h_0$ the identity, $h_1(K)=K'$, and $h_1(F)=F'$, preserving the given orientations. If $V$ and $V'$ are their Seifert matrices in any integral bases, then the basis transported by $h_1$ has matrix $V$, and any other target basis with transition matrix $P$ has matrix $V'=P^TVP$. Hence $V$ and $V'$ are S-equivalent, meaning they are related by a finite sequence of integral unimodular congruences and the two elementary rank-two enlargement moves or their reverses.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $L$ and $L'$ be nonempty oriented links in $S^3$ such
that some ambient isotopy of $S^3$ carries $L$ onto $L'$ and preserves the
orientations of the components
([[def-oriented-link-in-s-three-and-ambient-isotopy]]). Then the Alexander
modules $A_L$ and $A_{L'}$ of
[[def-one-variable-alexander-module-of-an-oriented-link]] are isomorphic as
$\Lambda$-modules over $\Lambda=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$, their zeroth elementary
ideals agree, $E_0(A_L)=E_0(A_{L'})$, and consequently the one-variable
Alexander polynomials of
[[def-alexander-polynomial-from-the-first-elementary-ideal]] satisfy
$$\Delta_{L'}(t)=\pm t^{k}\,\Delta_L(t)\quad\text{for some }k\in\mathbb Z;$$
so the oriented link type of $L$ determines $\Delta_L$ up to multiplication by
a unit $\pm t^k$ of $\Lambda$ (and, for knots, the Alexander invariant
$D_L=\Delta_L/(1-t)$ up to the same unit).

derivations.claim: Each plumbing has Euler characteristic $0+0-1=-1$, using a cell structure respecting the common square, since each annulus has Euler characteristic $0$ and the square has Euler characteristic $1$. Its boundary is one circle by the stipulated gluing, so $\chi=1-2g$ gives genus one. By [F3], $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$ is free of rank two. Choose any ordered basis $u,v$; [F2] makes its intersection matrix $J_0$ skew-symmetric and unimodular, hence $\det J_0=1$. Write the two core classes $a,b$ in this basis as the columns of an integer matrix $P$. The plumbing gives $a\cdot_F b=1$, so their intersection matrix is $J=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}=P^TJ_0P$. Taking determinants gives $1=(\det P)^2$, hence $\det P=\pm1$; therefore $a,b$ is an integral basis.

Equally oriented parallel cores of an annulus transport to its two induced boundary orientations with one reversed, so their linking is minus the boundary linking. Returning a small positive normal push in the complement of the other parallel core shows that each Hopf core self-pairing is minus its boundary linking. Thus the Hopf-band signs give $V_{11}=V_{22}=-1$ for $T$ and $V_{11}=-1,V_{22}=1$ for $E$. The specified disk bounded by $a^+$ is disjoint from $b$, so its class vanishes in the complement of $b$ and the linking definition gives $V_{12}=0$. Now that $a,b$ is a basis, [F2] yields $V_{12}-V_{21}=a\cdot_F b=1$, hence $V_{21}=-1$. This proves the displayed matrices.

For $V_T$, the matrix $V_T-tV_T^T$ is $\begin{pmatrix}t-1&t\\-1&t-1\end{pmatrix}$, with determinant $(1-t)^2+t=1-t+t^2$. For $V_E$, the matrix $V_E-tV_E^T$ is $\begin{pmatrix}t-1&t\\-1&1-t\end{pmatrix}$, with determinant $(t-1)(1-t)+t=-1+3t-t^2$. By [F4], these determinants represent $\Delta_T$ and $\Delta_E$ up to units. Substitution gives the stated values at $1$ and $-1$; every unit is $\pm t^k$, so the absolute values at both substitutions are independent of the representative. Their values $1$ at $1$ agree with [F5].

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Fix a coordinate orientation-reversing reflection $r:S^3\to S^3$ for the mirror convention. Let $K$ and $J$ be smooth oriented knots in the standard oriented three-sphere. A connected-sum datum consists of one smoothly embedded closed three-ball around a short subarc of $K$ and one around a short subarc of $J$, each meeting its knot in a single trivial properly embedded arc, together with the fixed standard orientation-reversing boundary identification of the two standard oriented ball boundaries that joins the oriented arcs into one circle. Choose this standard map once in the standard two-ball model so that it commutes with $r$ and an orientation-preserving half-turn interchanging the two balls preserves the joining convention. Here a trivial arc is an embedded interval in a ball that is carried by an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism of ball-arc pairs to a straight diameter. Remove the interiors of the two balls and glue the remaining boundary spheres using this fixed identification; the resulting oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere is a connected sum of $K$ and $J$, denoted $K\#J$ for the specified datum.

The **standard unknot** is the counterclockwise circle $U=\{(x_1,x_2,0)\in\mathbb R^3:x_1^2+x_2^2=1\}\subset S^3=\mathbb R^3\cup\{\infty\}$. Under inverse stereographic projection $x\mapsto(2x/(1+\lVert x\rVert^2),(\lVert x\rVert^2-1)/(1+\lVert x\rVert^2))$, this is the unit circle in the first coordinate two-plane of the unit sphere in $\mathbb R^4$. A knot is **nontrivial** if it is not ambient isotopic through orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms of $S^3$ to the standard unknot. A nontrivial knot is **prime** if it has no connected-sum presentation whose two summand knots are both nontrivial.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere $S^3$. A **Seifert surface** for $K$ is a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface $F\subset S^3$ with boundary set equal to $K$. Orient each boundary component so that an outward-pointing conormal in $F$, followed by a positive boundary tangent, is a positive basis of $TF$; the oriented boundary of $F$ must agree with the given orientation of $K$. For such a surface, its genus $g(F)$ is the unique nonnegative integer satisfying $\chi(F)=2-2g(F)-b$, where $b$ is the number of boundary components; here $b=1$, so $\chi(F)=1-2g(F)$. The compact-surface normal-form result supplies this integer under the stated choice axiom.

If $X$ is a nonempty contractible topological space, then for every $n\geq 0$
and every abelian group $G$,
$$H_n^{\mathrm{sing}}(X;G)\cong H_n^{\mathrm{sing}}(\ast;G),$$
where $\ast$ denotes a one-point space.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K:S^1\hookrightarrow S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere, and let $F\subset S^3$ be a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface with boundary $K$, oriented so that its boundary orientation is the given orientation of $K$. Let $g$ be the nonnegative integer determined by $\chi(F)=1-2g$. Choose an ordered integral basis $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ of the first singular homology group $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$, represented by integral one-cycles on $F$. Orient the normal line of $F$ by requiring $(n,u,v)$ to be positively oriented in $S^3$ whenever $(u,v)$ is a positive tangent basis of $F$. The positive push-off $a_i^+$ is the cycle carried to a sufficiently small positive normal level in a bicollar of $F$.

For disjoint oriented closed curves $J,L\subset S^3$, orient a meridian $\mu_L$ of $L$ so that a positive tangent to $L$ followed by a positive basis of its normal disk gives the ambient orientation. The linking number $\operatorname{lk}(J,L)$ is the integer determined by $[J]=\operatorname{lk}(J,L)[\mu_L]$ in $H_1(S^3\setminus L;\mathbb Z)$, using the Alexander-duality identification that sends $[\mu_L]$ to $1$. Extend linking additively over integral one-cycles. The Seifert pairing is $\theta_F(x,y)=\operatorname{lk}(x^+,y)$, and its matrix in the chosen basis is $V=(V_{ij})_{i,j=1}^{2g}$, where $V_{ij}=\theta_F(a_i,a_j)=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. The surface and basis are part of the data; this definition asserts no knot-only matrix invariant.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $L=K_1\cup\cdots\cup K_r\subset S^3$ be an
oriented link with $r\ge1$ components and complement $X_L$,
([[def-oriented-link-in-s-three-and-ambient-isotopy]]), and let
$$\varphi:H_1(X_L;\mathbb Z)\longrightarrow\mathbb Z$$
be the **total linking homomorphism**, defined as the composite
$$H_1(X_L;\mathbb Z)\xrightarrow[\ \sim\ ]{\mathrm{Alex}}\widetilde H^1(L;\mathbb Z)\cong\bigoplus_{i=1}^rH^1(K_i;\mathbb Z)\xrightarrow{\text{sum}}\mathbb Z,$$
where the first arrow is Alexander duality
([[thm-alexander-duality-for-compact-locally-contractible-subsets-of-a-sphere]]),
each $H^1(K_i;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$ is the orientation-induced
identification, and the last map sums the $r$ coordinates. By
[[prop-the-first-hurewicz-map-in-degree-one-is-abelianization]] the map $\varphi$
may again be written $\pi_1(X_L)\to H_1(X_L)\xrightarrow{\varphi}\mathbb Z$; we
denote both composites by $\varphi$ and set $K:=\ker\varphi$.

The **one-variable Alexander module** of $L$ is
$$A_L:=H_1(\widetilde{X_L};\mathbb Z),$$
the first singular homology of the connected infinite cyclic cover
$p:\widetilde{X_L}\to X_L$ classified by $K$
([[thm-classification-of-connected-covering-spaces]],
[[lem-subgroup-quotient-of-universal-cover]],
[[def-covering-map-and-evenly-covered-neighbourhoods]]), equipped with its
structure of module over $\Lambda=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$
([[def-the-laurent-polynomial-ring]]) in which $t$ acts by the deck
transformation corresponding to the positive generator of
$\operatorname{Deck}(\widetilde{X_L}/X_L)\cong\mathbb Z$.

**Caveats.** The cover is the one classified by $K=\ker\varphi$; since $K$ is
normal the cover is regular and its deck group is
$\pi_1(X_L)/K\cong\mathbb Z$
([[def-regular-covering]], [[thm-regular-covering-characterizations]], [[cor-deck-group-of-a-regular-covering]],
[[def-deck-transformation-and-deck-group]]). The module $A_L$ is ordinary
integral homology of the cover, with the deck action as its module structure;
no twisting by a representation of the link group is used. The total linking
homomorphism satisfies $\varphi(\mu_i)=1$ for a meridian $\mu_i$ of any one
component, so $r\ge1$ is needed for $\varphi$ to be interesting and $A_L$
depends on the orientations of all components through this map.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in the oriented standard three-sphere, let $F$ be a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface with boundary orientation equal to that of $K$, let $g$ satisfy $\chi(F)=1-2g$, and choose an ordered integral basis $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$. Use the positive normal convention $(n,u,v)>0$ and define $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. Let $A_K=H_1(\widetilde X_K;\mathbb Z)$ be the one-variable Alexander module of the knot complement $X_K=S^3\setminus K$, where the cover is classified by the total-linking homomorphism and $t$ acts by the deck transformation corresponding to the positive meridian. Then there is an isomorphism of $\Lambda=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$-modules
$$A_K\cong\operatorname{coker}\bigl(V-tV^T:\Lambda^{2g}\to\Lambda^{2g}\bigr).$$

Assume the full Axiom of Choice. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot, let $F\subset S^3$ be a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface with oriented boundary $K$, and let $\chi(F)=1-2g$ with $g\ge0$. Choose an ordered integral basis $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$, use the positive normal convention, and set $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. Let $\Lambda=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$, let $A_K$ be the first homology of the infinite cyclic cover classified by total linking with $t$ acting by the positive-meridian deck transformation, and let $\Delta_K$ be a generator of the zeroth elementary ideal $E_0(A_K)$. Then the square matrix $M(t)=V-tV^T$ generates that ideal:

$$E_0(A_K)=(\det M(t)).$$

For $g=0$, the matrix is empty and its determinant is $1$. In every genus, $\det(V-V^T)=\pm1$, so every generator $\Delta_K$ satisfies $\Delta_K(1)=\pm1$. The ideal and determinant assertions are compatible with integral basis changes and with orientation-preserving ambient isotopies of knot-surface pairs.

Assume the full Axiom of Choice. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot, and let $F\subset S^3$ be a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface whose oriented boundary is $K$, with $\chi(F)=1-2g$. Choose an ordered integral basis $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$ and use the positive normal convention $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. Let $A_K$ be the first homology of the infinite cyclic cover of $S^3\setminus K$ classified by total linking, with $t$ acting by the positive-meridian deck transformation. Let $\Delta_K(t)$ be the generator of the zeroth elementary ideal $E_0(A_K)$ in $\Lambda=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$, and write $p\doteq q$ when $p$ and $q$ differ by a unit $\pm t^k$ of $\Lambda$. Then for every such $F$ and basis,

$$\det(V-tV^T)\doteq\Delta_K(t).$$

The determinant is $1$ for the empty $0\times0$ matrix when $g=0$. This formula concerns the polynomial $\Delta_K$; the existing knot-normalized fraction $D_K=\Delta_K/(1-t)$ is a separate invariant.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, so that the Alexander module $A_L$ of an oriented
nonempty link $L$ is defined and finitely presented over
$\Lambda=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$
([[def-one-variable-alexander-module-of-an-oriented-link]],
[[lem-the-alexander-module-of-a-link-complement-is-finitely-presented]]). Let
$r$ be the number of components of $L$. Define the **one-variable Alexander
polynomial** $\Delta_L(t)\in\Lambda$ to be a greatest common divisor of the zeroth
elementary ideal $E_0(A_L)$
([[def-elementary-ideals-of-a-finitely-presented-module]]), i.e. a generator of
the smallest principal ideal of $\Lambda$ containing $E_0(A_L)$
([[lem-the-laurent-polynomial-ring-is-noetherian-and-a-unique-factorisation-domain]],
[[def-unique-factorisation-domain]]); it is well defined up to multiplication
by a unit $\pm t^k$ of $\Lambda$
([[lem-units-and-powers-of-the-laurent-polynomial-ring]]). The **Alexander
invariant** is the normalisation
$$D_L(t):=\begin{cases}\Delta_L(t),&r>1,\\[2pt] \dfrac{\Delta_L(t)}{1-t},&r=1,\end{cases}$$
understood for a knot as an element of the fraction field of $\Lambda$ when
$(1-t)\nmid\Delta_L(t)$; for the integer-valued link formulas of this page the
distinction matters and is stated with each use.

**Caveats.** The ideal $E_0(A_L)$ is a well-defined invariant of $L$ because
$A_L$ is finitely presented and elementary ideals are independent of the
presentation
([[lem-elementary-ideals-are-independent-of-the-presentation]]); a greatest
common divisor in a unique factorisation domain is well defined up to units, and
the units of $\Lambda$ are $\pm t^k$. For every link the absolute one-variable Alexander module admits a square
presentation, so $E_0(A_L)$ is principal, generated by its determinant (the
standard link fact recorded in [F3]). For a knot ($r=1$), every gcd
representative satisfies $\Delta_L(1)=\pm1$. These standard presentation and
normalisation facts are recorded here; the gcd definition itself uses only
finite presentability and unique factorisation.

Let $\mathbb Z[t]$ be the polynomial ring over the integers
([[def-polynomial-ring-over-a-commutative-ring]],
[[thm-polynomial-ring-is-a-commutative-ring]]) and let
$$S=\{t^k:k\ge0\}.$$
The set $S$ is multiplicative, and the **Laurent polynomial ring** is the
principal localisation
$$\Lambda_1:=\mathbb Z[t]_S=S^{-1}\mathbb Z[t]$$
([[def-principal-localisation]], [[def-multiplicative-subset-and-localisation]]).
It is a commutative ring with unit $1=t^0$ ([[def-commutative-ring]]). Write
again $t$ for the image of the indeterminate under the localisation map; then
$t$ is a unit with inverse $t^{-1}$
([[prop-units-in-a-localisation]]). Every element of $\Lambda_1$ has a
representative
$$\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}a_kt^k,\qquad a_k\in\mathbb Z,$$
with only finitely many nonzero coefficients, obtained by writing a fraction
$p/t^N$ as a finite $\mathbb Z$-linear combination of the powers
$t^{k-N}$; the finite coefficient sequence is unique: after multiplying two such sums
by a common sufficiently large power of $t$, equality becomes equality of
ordinary polynomials. The localisation map $\mathbb Z[t]\to\Lambda_1$ is
injective because $\mathbb Z[t]$ is a domain; hence their coefficients agree
([[cor-polynomial-ring-over-a-domain-is-a-domain]]). Equivalently, two such
sums are equal exactly when their coefficient sequences agree
([[prop-localisation-zero-equality-and-kernel-criteria]]).

**Universal property.** Let $A$ be a ring with unit and let
$\varphi\colon\mathbb Z[t]\to A$ be a unital ring homomorphism with
$\varphi(t)$ a unit of $A$. Then there is a unique unital ring homomorphism
$\widetilde\varphi\colon\Lambda_1\to A$ with
$\widetilde\varphi(t)=\varphi(t)$. Equivalently, for every unital ring $A$ and
every unit $u\in A$ there is a unique unital ring homomorphism
$\Lambda_1\to A$ with $t\mapsto u$ ([[thm-universal-property-of-localisation]],
[[def-ring-homomorphism]]).

The cited localisation theorem treats commutative target rings. For the
possibly noncommutative target used here, define
$\sum_k a_kt^k\mapsto\sum_k(a_k1_A)u^k$. Unique Laurent coefficients make
this well defined. Integer multiples of $1_A$ are central, and
$u^ku^l=u^{k+l}$ for all integers $k,l$, so finite distributivity proves
additivity, multiplicativity and preservation of $1$. Every unital
homomorphism must send $a_k$ to $a_k1_A$ and $t^k$ to $u^k$, proving
uniqueness. Taking $u=\varphi(t)$ gives the asserted extension of $\varphi$.

**Augmentation.** There is a unique unital ring homomorphism
$$\varepsilon\colon\Lambda_1\longrightarrow\mathbb Z,\qquad \varepsilon\Bigl(\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}a_kt^k\Bigr)=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}a_k,$$
the **sum-of-coefficients map** ([[thm-universal-property-of-localisation]]); it
is well defined because the coefficients are summable and their total sum is
unchanged along the relation of
[[prop-localisation-zero-equality-and-kernel-criteria]]. Its kernel is the
principal ideal $(t-1)$: indeed $\varepsilon(t-1)=0$, and if
$\varepsilon(x)=0$ then, writing $x=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}a_kt^k$ with finite
support and using that $\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}a_k=0$, one has
$$x=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}a_k(t^k-1)=(t-1)\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}a_k\,(1+t+\cdots+t^{k-1}),$$
where $1+t+\cdots+t^{k-1}$ denotes the empty sum $0$ for $k=0$ and, for
$k=-j<0$, the negative sum
$-(t^{-1}+t^{-2}+\cdots+t^{-j})$, so that
$t^{-j}-1=-(t-1)(t^{-1}+\cdots+t^{-j})$; hence $x\in(t-1)$, and the reverse
inclusion is $\varepsilon(t-1)=0$.

**Caveats.** This item realises $\Lambda_1$ by localisation and does **not**
identify it with an integral group ring: the additive group underlying
$\Lambda_1$ is $\bigoplus_{k\in\mathbb Z}\mathbb Z\,t^k$ and its multiplication
is the polynomial one ([[cor-polynomial-ring-over-a-domain-is-a-domain]] is not
needed for the ring laws but records that $\mathbb Z[t]$ is a domain). The
deck-module structures on homology introduced later on this page are defined
separately, by the universal property above.

Assume the full Axiom of Choice. Let $K,J\subset S^3$ be smooth oriented knots, and let $K\#J$ be their oriented connected sum for a connected-sum datum using the fixed gluing convention. Then

$$\Delta_{K\#J}(t)\doteq \Delta_K(t)\Delta_J(t),$$

where each $\Delta$ is the generator of the zeroth elementary ideal of the one-variable Alexander module and $\doteq$ means equality up to multiplication by a unit $\pm t^k$ of $\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$. The statement is independent of the local connected-sum choices and of the Seifert surfaces and bases used to compute the polynomials.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the full Axiom of Choice and let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot. For a nonzero Laurent polynomial $f(t)=\sum_j c_jt^j$, define $\deg f=\max\{j:c_j\ne0\}-\min\{j:c_j\ne0\}$; this is its exponent width and is unchanged by multiplication by a unit $\pm t^k$. Let $g(K)$ be the minimum genus of a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface in $S^3$ with oriented boundary $K$, and let $\Delta_K$ be any generator of the zeroth elementary ideal of its one-variable Alexander module. Then every such generator satisfies

$$\Delta_K(1)=\pm1,\qquad \Delta_K(t^{-1})\doteq\Delta_K(t),\qquad \deg\Delta_K\le 2g(K),$$

where $\doteq$ means equality up to a unit $\pm t^k$. Consequently, there is a unique associate $\Delta_K^\#(t)$ with $\Delta_K^\#(1)=1$ and $\Delta_K^\#(t^{-1})=\Delta_K^\#(t)$; its exponent support is centered in $[-g(K),g(K)]$. Under the existing convention the knot-normalized fraction $D_K(t)=\Delta_K(t)/(1-t)$ is distinct from the polynomial $\Delta_K$; because $\Delta_K(1)=\pm1$, it has a simple pole at $t=1$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $L$ and $L'$ be nonempty oriented links in $S^3$ such
that some ambient isotopy of $S^3$ carries $L$ onto $L'$ and preserves the
orientations of the components
([[def-oriented-link-in-s-three-and-ambient-isotopy]]). Then the Alexander
modules $A_L$ and $A_{L'}$ of
[[def-one-variable-alexander-module-of-an-oriented-link]] are isomorphic as
$\Lambda$-modules over $\Lambda=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$, their zeroth elementary
ideals agree, $E_0(A_L)=E_0(A_{L'})$, and consequently the one-variable
Alexander polynomials of
[[def-alexander-polynomial-from-the-first-elementary-ideal]] satisfy
$$\Delta_{L'}(t)=\pm t^{k}\,\Delta_L(t)\quad\text{for some }k\in\mathbb Z;$$
so the oriented link type of $L$ determines $\Delta_L$ up to multiplication by
a unit $\pm t^k$ of $\Lambda$ (and, for knots, the Alexander invariant
$D_L=\Delta_L/(1-t)$ up to the same unit).

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $(K,F)$ and $(K',F')$ be oriented knot and spanning-surface pairs in the oriented standard three-sphere, and let $h_t:S^3\to S^3$ be a smooth ambient isotopy with $h_0$ the identity, $h_1(K)=K'$, and $h_1(F)=F'$, preserving the given orientations. If $V$ and $V'$ are their Seifert matrices in any integral bases, then the basis transported by $h_1$ has matrix $V$, and any other target basis with transition matrix $P$ has matrix $V'=P^TVP$. Hence $V$ and $V'$ are S-equivalent, meaning they are related by a finite sequence of integral unimodular congruences and the two elementary rank-two enlargement moves or their reverses.

derivations.claim: By [A1] and [F9], the choice hypothesis of [F2] holds. The standard unknot $U$ bounds a hemisphere disk $D$ in a coordinate $2$-sphere in $S^3$, oriented to induce the chosen orientation of $U$. The disk contracts linearly to its center, so [F3] gives $H_1(D;\mathbb Z)=0$. Its basis is empty, so its Seifert matrix is $0\times0$ and its determinant is $1$ by [F4]. The matrix theorem and local E0 lemma in [F5] give $\Delta_U\doteq1$; by [F10] choose the representative $\Delta_U=1$. By [F11] the computation applies to the oriented unknot type, independently of the chosen representative.

By [F6], $D_U(t)=1/(1-t)$. If $D_U$ belonged to $\Lambda$, there would be $q(t)\in\Lambda$ with $(1-t)q(t)=1$. Applying [F7] gives $0=1$ in $\mathbb Z$, a contradiction. Thus $D_U$ is not a Laurent polynomial.

By [F8], $\Delta_{U\#U}\doteq\Delta_U^2\doteq1$. Any representative of $D_{U\#U}$ therefore has the form $\pm t^k/(1-t)$, whose numerator evaluates to $\pm1$ at $t=1$; applying [F7] as in step 2.1 shows it is not in $\Lambda$.
